4 5. Preparing Data

4.1 5.a. Reading data file to rds
We first read the input data sets that is saved in simple feature data frame.

mdata <- read_rds("data/rawdata/mdata.rds")


glimpse(mdata)



4.2 5.b. Data Sampling
We split the entire data into 65% training and 35% test by using initial_split() of rsample package, which belongs to tigymodels ecosystem.
Later we extract the training set and test set from a data split object created by functions initial_split().

set.seed(1234)
resale_split <- initial_split(mdata, prop = 6.5/10,)
train_data <- training(resale_split)
test_data <- testing(resale_split)

We save both files.

write_rds(train_data, "data/model/train_data.rds")
write_rds(test_data, "data/model/test_data.rds")



4.3 5.c. Computing Correlation Matrix
Before loading predictors into a predictive model, let’s plot the correlation matrix to check if there is any sign of multicolinearity

mdata_nogeo <- st_drop_geometry(mdata)
corrplot::corrplot(cor(mdata_nogeo[, 2:17]),
                   diag = FALSE, # hide diagonal or TRUE
                   order = "AOE",# angular order of the eigenvectors" /original/AOE/FPC/hclust/alphabet
                   tl.pos = "td", # text label position: top and diagonal/lt/n null
                   tl.cex = 0.5,  # text label size: shrinks 50%
                   method = "number",  # display number/circle/color/shade/pie
                   type = "upper") #show only the upper triangle/full/lower

There is no sign of multicolinearity since all correlation values are below 0.8.

section: 6 7. Building a Non-spatial Multiple Linear Regression
text:
6 7. Building a Non-spatial Multiple Linear Regression
A multiple regression model is built as a base line model.

price_mlr <- lm(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +                   
                  storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
                  PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
                  PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
                  PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                  WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
                  WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
                data=train_data)
summary(price_mlr)

This linear regression model shows a strong explanatory power, accounting for about 73.7% of the variation in HDB resale prices. The key determinants include structural factors such as floor area (adding roughly $2,781 per sqm) and storey height (adding about $14,299 per level). Locational attributes also play a major role — proximity to MRT stations, the CBD, and hawker centres notably increases resale values. Overall, the model highlights that both physical characteristics and accessibility to amenities are critical in shaping HDB resale prices across Singapore.

write_rds(price_mlr, "data/model/price_mlr.rds" )

title: Hands on Exercise 8 : Geographically Weighted Predictive Models
text:
7 8. gwr Predictive Method
We now build and calibrate geographically weighted regression model to predict the HDB resales prices using methods from GWmodel package.
Computing Predicted Values of the Test Data suggests that we need to convert the data to spatial objects first. Convert the training and test data into SpatialPointDateFrame for use in GWR:

train_data_sp <- as(train_data, "Spatial")
test_data_sp <- as(test_data, "Spatial")
train_data_sp
test_data_sp


7.1 8.a. Computing Adaptive Bandwidth
We use the bw.gwr() function from the GWmodel package to determine the optimal bandwidth. The “CV” (Cross Validation) method is chosen for calibration because, between the two available options “CV” and “AIC”, the CV method generally produces a smaller bandwidth, allowing the model to capture more local variation in the data.
The code chunk below computes and saves the optimal bandwidth. The search can be time consuming and computationally intensive.

bw_adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_sp,
  approach="CV",
  kernel="gaussian",
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat=FALSE)


write_rds(bw_adaptive, "data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")

We’ve found optimal bandwidth is 40 neighour points.


7.2 8.b. Constructing the Adaptive Bandwidth GWR Model
Let us call the save bandwidth by using the code chunk below.

bw_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")


bw_adaptive

Then we build the GWR-based hedonic pricing model using adaptive bandwidth and Gaussian kernel. Same reason as the previous step, we save a copy of the gwrm file.

gwr_adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_sp,
  bw=bw_adaptive, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
write_rds(gwr_adaptive, 
          "data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")



7.3 8.c. Retrieve gwr Output Object
We re-load the saved gwrm object and retrieve the report of model output.

gwr_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")


gwr_adaptive

The report reads that R2 value has increased from 0.7373 to 0.9677 indicating model’s fit has substantially proved and information loss has decreased as AICc down from 257320.3 to 238871.8.


7.4 8.d. Computing Adaptive Bandwidth for the Test Data

gwr_bw_test_adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=test_data_sp,
  approach="CV", #   note we use approach="CV" compared with bw=bw_adaptive in training
  kernel="gaussian",
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat=FALSE)

write_rds(gwr_bw_test_adaptive, 
          "data/model/gwr_bw_test_adaptive.rds")

The Cross-validation determines the optimal adaptive bandwidth is 25 for the test set.


7.5 8.e. Computing Predicted Values of the Test Data

gwr_pred <- gwr.predict(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + 
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + 
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + 
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, 
  data=train_data, 
  predictdata = test_data, 
  bw=40, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  adaptive=TRUE, 
  longlat = FALSE)

write_rds(gwr_pred, 
          "data/model/gwr_pred.rds")

8 9. Calibrating Random Forest Model
Now, we calibrate the model by using random forest function from ranger package.

8.1 9.a. Preparing Coordinates Data
First we calculate x,y coordinates matrix for whole dataset, and training and test sets.

train_data <- read_rds("data/model/train_data.rds")
test_data <- read_rds("data/model/test_data.rds")


coords <- st_coordinates(mdata)
coords_train <- st_coordinates(train_data)
coords_test <- st_coordinates(test_data)


coords_train <- write_rds(coords_train, "data/geospatial/coords_train.rds" )
coords_test <- write_rds(coords_test, "data/geospatial/coords_test.rds" )



8.2 9.b. Dropping Geometry Field
The geometry column should be removed since it is not required for the upcoming analysis. The code chunk below uses st_drop_geometry() function from the sf package to drop the geometry.

train_data_nogeom <- train_data %>% st_drop_geometry()
test_data_nogeom <- test_data %>% st_drop_geometry()



8.3 9.c. Calibrating a Non-spatial Random Forest Model

set.seed(1234)
rf <- ranger(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + 
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS +  
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_nogeom)

rf

The Ranger result shows our R2 value is 0.9496 that is much higher than non-spatial regression model.

write_rds(rf, "data/model/rf.rds")

section: 9 10. Calibrating Geographical Weighted Random Forest Model
text:
9 10. Calibrating Geographical Weighted Random Forest Model
Next we grf() of SpatialML package to calibrate a geographic random forest model.

9.1 10.a. Calibrating Using Training Data
We apply grf() of SpatialML package to calibrate model on training data.

set.seed(1234)
gwRF_adaptive <- grf(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  dframe=train_data_nogeom, 
  bw=40,
  kernel="adaptive",
  coords=coords_train)

R2 on the training set is 0.9515.
We again save the new model on training data.

write_rds(gwRF_adaptive, "data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")

Then we retrieve the model for next steps.

gwRF_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")



9.2 10.b. Predicting by using Test Data

9.2.1 10.b.1. Preparing the Test Data
Now we use cbind() to combine test_data and coords_test and remove the geometry.

test_data_nogeom <- cbind(test_data, coords_test)%>%
  st_drop_geometry()



9.2.2 10.b.2. Predicting with Test Data
Next, We use predict.grf() of SpatialML package to predict the resale price using gwPF_adaptive model on the test data.

gwRF_pred <- predict.grf(gwRF_adaptive, 
                        test_data_nogeom, 
                        x.var.name="X",
                        y.var.name="Y", 
                        local.w=1,
                        global.w=0)


GRF_pred <- write_rds(gwRF_pred, "data/model/GRF_pred.rds")



9.2.3 10.b.3. Converting the Predicting Output into a data.frame
We reload the saved predicting output (generated from predict.grf() in the previous step) back to R and convert it into a data frame for further study since the original output is in numeric format.

GRF_pred <- read_rds("data/model/GRF_pred.rds")
GRF_pred_df <- as.data.frame(GRF_pred)


glimpse(GRF_pred_df)

To compare the actual and predicted, we combine the with GRF_pred_df and select required columns: resale_pricein test_data and GRF_pred the column where predicting outputs are in GRF_pred_df into a new data frame called test_data_p and save it on the disk.

test_data_p <- cbind(test_data, GRF_pred_df) %>%
  select(resale_price, GRF_pred)


glimpse(test_data_p)
write_rds(test_data_p,"data/model/test_data_p.rds")



9.2.4 10.b.4. Calculating Root Mean Square Error
To measure the difference between actual and predicted in the regression model, we use rmse() of Metrics package to compute the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). The RMSE is 28160.87 for this GWR model.

rmse(test_data_p$resale_price, test_data_p$GRF_pred)



9.2.5 10.b.5. Visualising the Predicted Values
Alternatively, we use scatterplot to visualise how far the predicted values deviate from the actual ones using the functions geom_point() and ggplot().
For the reference line, we use geom_abline() to create a 45-degree line in the positive quadrant by setting the arguments slope = 1 and intercept = 0. To customise the line style, we can specify the linetype argument using numeric values or their names: 0: blank 1: solid (default) 2: dashed 3: dotted 4: dotdash 5: longdash 6: twodash

ggplot(data = test_data_p, aes(x= GRF_pred, y = resale_price)) +
  geom_point() +
 geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 1, size = 0.8)

Based on the visual analysis, the scatterplot indicates that the model achieves strong predictive accuracy, as most data points closely align with the 45-degree reference line. This tight clustering suggests a high level of agreement between the predicted and actual resale prices. Additionally, the plot shows only a few noticeable outliers, implying that prediction errors are generally minimal and the model performs reliably across most observations.

Hands on Exercise 9 : Modelling Geographic of Accessibility
text:
We’re going to model geographic accessibility, which is basically how easy it is for people to get to a specific place or service. We’ll measure this using travel time and distance in R.



Import GIS polygon data into R and save them as simple feature data frame by using appropriate functions of sf package of R;
Import aspatial data into R and save them as simple feature data frame by using appropriate functions of sf package of R;
Computer accessibility measure by using Hansen’s potential model and Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM); and
Visualise the accessibility measures by using tmap and ggplot2 packages.







Dataset Name
Description
Format




MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL
URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundary GIS data, downloaded from data.gov.sg.
ERSI Shapefile


hexagons
A 250m radius hexagons GIS data, created by using st_make_grid() of sf package.
ESRI shapefile


ELDERCARE
Locations of eldercare service, downloaded from data.gov.sg. Two formats were available, ESRI shapefile and Google KML. The Shapefile format was selected as it is a geospatial-native format that preserves coordinate systems and spatial attributes more accurately.
ESRI shapefile


OD_Matrix
A travel distance matrix between the origin hexagon cells and eldercare service locations, measured by metres. It includes:

origin_id: hexagon identifier
destination_id: eldercare facility identifier
entry_cost: perpendicular distance from the origin to nearest road entry
network_cost: actual travel distance on the road
exit_cost: perpendicular distance from destination to nearest road connection
total_cost: total travel cost, computed as entry_cost+network_cost+exit_cost

Likewise, we add a capacity field for the eldercare layer, which indicates the service capacity or supply at each facility (e.g., number of beds or service slots available).
For the purpose of this exercise, both demand and capacity are assigned a constant value of 100 to simplify the demonstration. In practice, actual population data and real facility capacity figures should be used.

  mutate(capacity = 100)

  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)

5 5. Hansen Method
ac() computes spatial accessibility of demand locations (e.g., residential areas) to service locations (e.g., eldercare centres). It implements several well-known measures:

“Hansen”:Hansen gravity-type accessibility
“KD2SFCA”: Kernel/Downgraded 2SFCA (distance-decay)
“SAM”: Spatial Accessibility Measure

Usage:

ac(p, n, D, d0, power=2, family=“SAM”)

Arguments:

p: numeric vector of demand at each origin (e.g., number of senior residents per hexagon).
n: numeric vector of supply at each destination (e.g., number of beds per eldercare centre).
D: distance or time matrix separating origins (rows) from destinations (columns). Prefer road-network distance or travel time.
d0: catchment threshold (distance/time) defining which OD pairs “count”.
power: distance-decay exponent (commonly 2 in gravity models).
family: which accessibility method to compute: “SAM”, “2SFCA”, “KD2SFCA”, or “Hansen” (default “SAM”).

All four methods are gravity-based accessibility measures where accessibility improves with greater service capacity and proximity, and decreases with distance and population demand due to competition for limited resources.
Return value
A numeric vector of accessibility scores for each origin (length = length(p)).

             bbox = mapex) + 
      tm_polygons(fill = col_name,

      tm_shape(eldercare) +

              fill = "red",
              col = "black") +
      tm_title(paste("Hansen Accessibility - Power =", power_val)) +
      tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +

      tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
  )

Power = 0.5 Weak distance decay - accessibility spreads widely across Singapore, creating a smooth pattern with minimal variation between near and far locations.
Power = 1.0 Moderate decay - clearer concentration around facilities emerges, but surrounding areas still maintain reasonable accessibility with visible gradients.
Power = 1.5 Strong decay - steep accessibility drop-off creates distinct service zones around each facility, highlighting spatial inequality between central and peripheral areas.
Power = 2.0 Very strong decay - accessibility highly localized immediately around facilities, with large regions showing near-zero access and sharp peaks at facility locations.
Power = 2.5 Extreme decay - accessibility limited to immediate facility vicinity, vast majority of Singapore shows minimal access, emphasizing critical importance of proximity.
As the power parameter increases, accessibility becomes increasingly concentrated around eldercare facilities due to stronger distance decay. Lower powers (0.5-1.0) create more equitable but potentially overestimated accessibility, while higher powers (1.5-2.5) produce highly localized patterns that better reflect distance friction but may underestimate access for intermediate distances. The choice of power value represents a trade-off between modeling realistic distance barriers and capturing broader spatial accessibility patterns.

We first read the input data sets that is saved in simple feature data frame.

mdata <- read_rds("data/rawdata/mdata.rds")



3.2 2.b.2. Data Sampling
Calibrating predictive models are computational intensive, especially random forest method is used. For quick prototyping, a 10% sample will be selected at random from the data by using the code chunk below,

set.seed(1234)
HDB_sample <- mdata %>%
  sample_n(1500)







Warning



When using GWmodel to calibrate explanatory or predictive models, it is very important to ensure that there are no overlapping point features


The code chunk below is used to check if there are overlapping point features.

overlapping_points <- HDB_sample %>%
  mutate(overlap = lengths(st_equals(., .))>1)



3.3 2.b.3. Spatial Jitter
In the code chunk below, ‘st_jitter()’ of sf package is used to move the point features by 5m to avoid overlapping point features.

HDB_sample <- HDB_sample %>%
  st_jitter(amount = 1)



3.4 2.b.4. Data Sampling including spatial sampling
The entire data are split into training and test data sets with 65% and 35% respectively by using initial_split() of rsample package. rsample is one of the package of tigymodels.

set.seed(1234)
resale_split <- initial_split(HDB_sample, 
                              prop = 6.67/10,)
train_data <- training(resale_split)
test_data <- testing(resale_split)



3.5 2.b.5. Computing Adaptive Bandwidth
We use the bw.gwr() function from the GWmodel package to determine the optimal bandwidth. The “CV” (Cross Validation) method is chosen for calibration because, between the two available options “CV” and “AIC”, the CV method generally produces a smaller bandwidth, allowing the model to capture more local variation in the data.
The code chunk below computes and saves the optimal bandwidth. The search can be time consuming and computationally intensive.

bw_adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_sp,
  approach="CV",
  kernel="gaussian",
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat=FALSE)


write_rds(bw_adaptive, "data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")

We’ve found optimal bandwidth is 40 neighour points.


3.6 2.b.6. Constructing the Adaptive Bandwidth GWR Model
Let us call the save bandwidth by using the code chunk below.

bw_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")

Then we build the GWR-based hedonic pricing model using adaptive bandwidth and Gaussian kernel. Same reason as the previous step, we save a copy of the gwrm file.

gwr_adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_sp,
  bw=bw_adaptive, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
write_rds(gwr_adaptive, 
          "data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")



3.7 2.b.7. Retrieve gwr Output Object
We re-load the saved gwrm object and retrieve the report of model output.

gwr_adaptive


The report when we use GW model, Global is least squared model, Localised one is Geographically Weighted Regression and then use it for calibration purpose
For explanatory model, take the whole data and compare the Significance stars (least squared model, Adjusted R2) and Diagnostic information.
Adjusted R2 is 0.95822 in GWR model Diagnostic much better than Global regression Significance stars Adjusted R2 0.7387.



3.8 2.b.8. Street name which starts with ST. replace with Saint

HDBresale$street_name <- gsub(
  "ST\\.","SAINT",
  HDBresale$street_name)


geocode <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  address <- paste(block,streetname,sep = " ")
  query <- list("searchVal"= address,
                "returnGeom"= "Y",
                "getAddrDetails"= "N", #make it Y if you want full address
                "pageNum"="1")
  
  res <- GET(base_url, query = query)
  restext<- content(res, as="text")
  
  output<- fromJSON(restext) %>%
    as.data.frame %>%
    select(results.LATITUDE, results.LONGITUDE)
  
  return(output)
}



3.9 2.b.9. Read all the records , return the geocode , insert the value into HDBresale dataframe

HDBresale$LATITUDE <- 0
HDBresale$LONGITUDE <- 0 

for(i in 1:nrow(HDBresale)){
  temp_output <- geocode(HDBresale[i,4], HDBresale[i,5])
  
  HDBresale$LATITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LATITUDE
  HDBresale$LONGITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LONGITUDE
}



3.10 2.b.10. Convert HDBresale(13 columns) to spatial data (HDBresale_sf) which is geometry area , make sure it is in SVY 21 projection

# Convert to spatial data frame
HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
                         crs = 4326) %>%  # WGS84 for lat/lon coordinates
  st_transform(crs = 3414)  # Transform to SVY21 projection (EPSG:3414)

# Check the result
print(HDBresale_sf)



3.11 2.b.11. Preschool data

preschool = st_read("data/rawdata/PreSchoolsLocation.kml") %>% 
  st_transform(crs=3414)

All spatial data are measured in meters. Therefore, when we perform a proximity search within 1 km (equivalent to 1000 meters), the result will return either TRUE or FALSE, depending on whether a point falls within that distance. We can then count the number of TRUE and FALSE values. The same logic is applied for identifying childcare centers, kindergartens, and bus stops located within 350 meters.

  HDBresale_sf, preschool, dist = 350)

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(prischool_350m = map_int(within_350m,length))

The KML file MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml was successfully loaded using the KML driver. It contains a simple feature collection of 332 multipolygon features with two attribute fields. Each feature corresponds to a URA Master Plan 2019 subzone (excluding sea areas) and is defined using two-dimensional geographic coordinates (longitude and latitude) under the WGS 84 coordinate system. extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_) # check if text is na
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr") # find table row element 
  
  value <- rows %>%
    # looks through each row to find table header == field_name and
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>% 
    html_element("td") %>% # extract table data
    html_text2() # and then extract clean text context
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value # return value if is not NA
}

  select(-Name, -Description) %>% # unselect columns "Name" and "Description"
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col()) # move the "geometry" to the end

5.3 5.c. Exploratory Analysis for All Three Selected Sectors
Purpose:
After geocoding and preparing the data, the next step is to explore the distribution of new business registrations for all three selected sectors (SSIC 56111, 56102, 56301). This allows us to understand temporal trends (when businesses were registered) and spatial patterns (where businesses are concentrated). Comparing sectors can reveal which types of businesses are growing faster and which areas of Singapore attract more of certain business types.
Analysis Goals:

Show monthly registration trends for each sector in early 2025.
Map the spatial locations of all new businesses with different colors or symbols to distinguish sectors.
Prepare the dataset so that further spatio-temporal analysis (KDE, second-order analysis) can be applied efficiently.


5.3.1 5.c.1. Combining the Three Sectors

# Filter and combine the three sectors
selected_ssic <- c(56111, 56102, 56301)

biz_all <- acra_data %>%
  select(1:24) %>%
  filter(primary_ssic_code %in% selected_ssic) %>%
  rename(date = registration_incorporation_date) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date),
         YEAR = year(date),
         MONTH_NUM = month(date),
         MONTH_ABBR = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
         postal_code = str_pad(postal_code, width = 6, side = "left", pad = "0"),
         sector = case_when(
           primary_ssic_code == 56111 ~ "Cafes/Restaurants",
           primary_ssic_code == 56102 ~ "Food Catering Services",
           primary_ssic_code == 56301 ~ "Bars/Pubs"
         )) %>%
  filter(YEAR == 2025)

Explanation:
We first select the three sectors of interest and create a new column sector with descriptive labels. This makes later analysis and visualization clearer. We also ensure postal codes are padded for geocoding and restrict the data to the first half of 2025.

5.3.2 5.c.2. Geocoding Postal Codes

# Extract unique postal codes
postcodes <- unique(biz_all$postal_code)

# Initialize dataframes
found <- data.frame()
not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character())

# Loop through postal codes to query OneMap API
for (pc in postcodes) {
  query <- list(
    searchVal = pc,
    returnGeom = "Y",
    getAddrDetails = "Y",
    pageNum = "1"
  )
  
  res <- GET("https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search", query = query)
  json <- content(res)
  
  if (json$found != 0) {
    df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    df$input_postcode <- pc
    found <- bind_rows(found, df)
  } else {
    not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc))
  }
}

# Keep relevant columns
found <- found %>% select(1:10)

# Merge geocoded results with business dataset
biz_all <- biz_all %>%
  left_join(found, by = c('postal_code' = 'POSTAL'))

# Convert to spatial object
biz_all_sf <- st_as_sf(biz_all, coords = c("X","Y"), crs=3414)

Explanation:
This step ensures that each business has spatial coordinates for mapping. The OneMap API is used to geocode postal codes, and the resulting coordinates are merged back into the business dataset. Converting it to an sf object allows the use of geospatial functions in tmap and other R spatial packages.

5.4 6. Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Analysis

5.4.1 6.a. Why KDE and Spatio-Temporal Analysis?

Purpose:
While the EDA gives a basic sense of “where” and “when” businesses are located, KDE helps us quantify density patterns and identify hotspots of business activity.
First-order spatial patterns:
KDE estimates the intensity of points across a continuous surface. This shows areas with unusually high concentrations of businesses.

Spatio-temporal patterns:
Incorporating time allows us to see how hotspots evolve across months. This helps answer:

Are some areas consistently popular for new businesses?
Are certain sectors growing faster in particular locations?


Policy Implication:
Planners can use these patterns to improve land use planning, allocate resources efficiently, and support targeted economic initiatives.

5.4.2 6.b. Spatial and Spatio-Temporal KDE for Selected Sectors

library(spatstat)
library(sparr)

# Define Singapore bounding box (in projected CRS)
bbox <- st_bbox(biz_selected_sf)
window <- owin(xrange = c(bbox["xmin"], bbox["xmax"]),
               yrange = c(bbox["ymin"], bbox["ymax"]))

# KDE for each sector
kde_results <- list()
for(sec in unique(biz_selected_sf$sector)){
  sector_sf <- biz_selected_sf %>% filter(sector == sec)
  
  # Convert to ppp object
  coords <- st_coordinates(sector_sf)
  ppp_obj <- ppp(x = coords[,1], y = coords[,2], window = window)
  
  # KDE (adjust sigma as needed)
  kde_res <- density(ppp_obj, sigma = 200)  # example bandwidth in meters
  kde_results[[sec]] <- kde_res
}

# Plot KDEs side by side
par(mfrow = c(1, length(kde_results)))
for(sec in names(kde_results)){
  plot(kde_results[[sec]], main = paste("KDE -", sec))
}

title: Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore
text:
Urban mobility refers to the movement of people and goods within and between cities, spanning all modes of transport such as walking, cycling, public transit, private vehicles, and freight. Driven by factors like population growth and climate change, urban mobility planning aims to create smart, efficient, and sustainable networks that reduce congestion and emissions while enhancing quality of life and economic vitality.
As city-wide urban infrastructures become digital, the datasets obtained can be used as a framework for tracking movement patterns through space and time. This is especially true with the widespread deployment of pervasive computing technologies such as smart cards, GPS, and RFID in vehicles. For example, routes and ridership data were collected with the use of smart cards and Global Positioning System (GPS) devices available on the public buses. These large-scale movement datasets often contain patterns that reveal important characteristics of urban mobility.
In real-world practices, the use of these massive locational aware data to gain better urban mobility patterns and trends, however, tend to be confined to simple tracking and mapping with GIS applications. This is mainly because conventional GIS tools lack robust geospatial statistics capabilities for analyzing and modeling spatial and spatio-temporal data.

This exercise applies advanced geospatial statistical methods to:


Apply Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) including Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi* to identify spatial clusters and outliers in bus passenger boarding patterns

Conduct Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) to understand how passenger demand hotspots evolve over time across different periods of the week

Provide data-driven insights for urban transport planning and service optimization in Singapore

Compute Getis-Ord Gi* statistics for hotspot detection# Gi* identifies statistically significant hotspots and coldspots

    Afternoon_Hotspot = ifelse(Afternoon_Gi > 1.96 & !is.na(Afternoon_Gi), "Hot Spot", "Not Significant"),

title: In class Exercise 10 : Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
Market area analysis (also known as Trade Area Analysis) is the process of defining and studying the geographical area from which a business draws its customers. It involves analyzing data on consumer demographics, spending habits, and competitors to understand market viability, identify opportunities, and inform decisions about location, marketing, and expansion. It often combines empirical observation, like customer spotting, with mathematical models to identify market segments and understand customer behavior.
Huff model is a geospatial analysis method commonly used in market area analysis to predict the probability that a consumer from a specific area will patronize a particular store, based on the store’s attractiveness and distance relative to competitors. It calculates a store’s market share by considering factors like size or sales for attractiveness and distance or travel time, with the probability decreasing as distance or competition increases. This tool helps businesses assess potential revenue, define trade areas, and make informed decisions about site selection
